_meta.purpose: Stage 1 calibration set for Phase 4 (prompt completeness scoring). Used to sanity-check that Layer 2's LLM critique separates vague prompts from thorough ones before shipping it — run a handful of these through /api/score/critique and compare the LLM's per-dimension verdicts against `expectedPresent` below.
_meta.note: Only 6 real sessions existed in production at the time this was built (site launched same day as this phase). The 6 marked source:'real' below are those, pulled verbatim. The other 24 are synthetic — written to deliberately span the vague-to-thorough spectrum, which is more useful for calibration than waiting on organic traffic to reach 50. Recalibrate against real sessions once volume grows; don't treat these synthetic scores as ground truth for user behavior, only as a spread of clear-cut cases for spotting a miscalibrated LLM grader.
_meta.scoredBy: AI-assisted (Claude), not independently human-verified — spot-check before relying on this for a go/no-go call on Layer 2's system prompt.

examples.originalPrompt: Draft an email to our newsletter subscribers announcing a 20%-off weekend sale. Audience is existing customers who've bought from us before. Keep it under 150 words, casual and warm tone, and include one clear call-to-action button text suggestion. Here's context: we're a small candle company, this is our first-ever sale, and we want to avoid sounding desperate or overly salesy.
examples.note: Missing only a concrete example and explicit success criteria.

examples.originalPrompt: Write a product description for a smart water bottle. Audience: fitness-focused millennials shopping on Amazon. Format: 100-150 words, 3 bullet feature points, punchy first line. Context: the bottle tracks hydration via an app, has a 24-hour temperature hold, and this is a mid-market brand (not luxury, not budget). Constraint: don't use the word 'revolutionary' or make unverified health claims. Here's an example of a listing tone we like: 'Meet the bottle that remembers to drink water so you don't have to.' Success looks like: a shopper stops scrolling and adds it to cart within one read.
examples.note: Ceiling case — every dimension explicitly present.

examples.originalPrompt: Explain quantum entanglement
examples.note: No audience given — 'explain to whom' is the single biggest missing lever here per the checklist.

examples.originalPrompt: Explain quantum entanglement to a curious 10-year-old, in about 4 sentences, using an everyday analogy rather than equations
examples.note: 'using an everyday analogy rather than equations' reads as a constraint (what to avoid: equations).

examples.originalPrompt: Give me feedback on this cover letter: [pasted text]. I'm applying for a UX design internship at a startup. Tell me if it's too long, whether the tone matches a startup culture, and flag anything that sounds generic or AI-written.
examples.note: The three explicit checks requested (length, tone-fit, genericness) function as success criteria; the pasted letter is context, not an example of desired output.
